\section{Networks}

% Generated by scripts/blueprint_from_docstring.py from TCSlib.GraphTheory.Core.Networks.
% Prose is extracted from Lean docstrings; verbatim book quotations are excluded.

\begin{definition}[A network $N = (D, X, Y, c)$]
\lean{Networks.Network}
\label{Networks.Network}
\leanok
A transportation network: goods are produced at the sources, consumed
at the sinks, and shipped along the arcs, each with a maximum throughput.

\textbf{!} Missing from Mathlib (0 hits for flow/network/capacity).
Capacity is carried as a \emph{function} \texttt{cap : V $\to$ V $\to$ $\mathbb{N}$}, with \texttt{cap u v = 0} encoding
"no arc $u \to v$"; this makes $f^{+}$/$f^{-}$ plain \texttt{Finset.sum}s.  \textbf{!} It cannot represent
\textbf{parallel arcs}, which is a real restriction --- lemma 11.4 is about a network in
which every arc has unit capacity, and B&M's digraphs may have several arcs between
the same pair.

The structure carries \textbf{both} $X$, $Y$ (the source/sink \emph{sets} of \S{}11.1) and the
distinguished $x$, $y$ used from \S{}11.2 onward.  That is because the book reduces
the first to the second: *adjoin two new vertices $x$ and $y$; join $x$ to each
vertex in $X$ by an arc of capacity $\infty$; join each vertex in $Y$ to $y$ by an arc
of capacity $\infty$; designate $x$ as the source and $y$ as the sink of $N'$* --- after
which *throughout the next three sections, we shall confine our attention to
networks that have a single source $x$ and a single sink $y$*.  That reduction is
exercise 11.1.4, which is deferred here (it needs an $\mathbb{N}\infty$-capacity parallel
carrier), so the two are simply both recorded in the structure.

\textbf{\textbf{!} Structural defect: $x$, $y$ are unrelated to $X$, $Y$.}  Nothing in the
structure requires \texttt{N.x $\in$ N.X}, let alone \texttt{N.X = \{N.x\}}.  But \texttt{val} is defined over
the \emph{set} $X$ while every \S{}11.2--\S{}11.3 result is about cuts separating the single
$x$ from the single $y$.  The two therefore measure different things, and \textbf{lemma
11.1, theorem 11.1 in both forms, corollary 11.1 and theorem 11.3 are all false as
stated}.

\emph{Counterexample} (one network refutes all of them).  $V = {x_{1}, x_{2}, y_{1}}$,
$X = {x_{1}, x_{2}}$, $Y = {y_{1}}$, \texttt{N.x = x$_{1}$}, \texttt{N.y = y$_{1}$}; capacities $c(x_{1},y_{1}) = c(x_{2},y_{1}) = 1$
and $0$ elsewhere.  Then $I = \emptyset$, so any $f$ within capacity is a flow; take
$f(x_{1},y_{1}) = f(x_{2},y_{1}) = 1$.
\item \texttt{val f = f$^{+}$(X) - f$^{-}$(X) = 2}.
\item $S = {x_{1}}$ is a cut ($x_{1} \in S$, $y_{1} \notin S$), with $f^{+}(S) - f^{-}(S) = 1$ and
  \texttt{cap S = 1}.
\item So lemma 11.1 asserts $2 = 1$; theorem 11.1 asserts $2 \le 1$.
\item Max flow value is $2$, minimum cut capacity is $1$, so theorem 11.3 asserts
  $2 = 1$.
\item Corollary 11.1 fails too: $f'(x_{1},y_{1}) = 1$, $f'(x_{2},y_{1}) = 0$ has
  \texttt{val f' = 1 = cap\{x$_{1}$\}}, yet $f'$ is not a maximum flow.

\emph{The repair} is to add the fields \texttt{hx : N.X = \{N.x\}} and \texttt{hy : N.Y = \{N.y\}} to the
structure (the book's standing convention for \S{}\S{}11.2--11.4), or equivalently to add
them as hypotheses on the affected theorems.  The \S{}11.1 results --- exercises 11.1.2
and 11.1.3 --- are unaffected and should keep the general $X$, $Y$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Intermediate vertices $I = V \ (X \cup Y)$]
\lean{Networks.Network.I}
\label{Networks.Network.I}
\leanok
\uses{Networks.Network}
The transit points of the network, which neither produce nor consume.
The conservation condition (11.2) applies exactly here --- what flows in must flow
out --- and that is what makes \texttt{val f} well defined (exercise 11.1.3).

\texttt{Finset.univ \textbackslash\{\} (X $\cup$ Y)}, so $I$ is a \texttt{Finset} and membership is
decidable --- needed by \texttt{IsFlow}'s second clause.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[$f^{+}(S) = f(S, \bar{S}) = \sum_{u\in S} \sum_{v\notin S} f u v$]
\lean{Networks.Network.fOut}
\label{Networks.Network.fOut}
\leanok
\uses{Networks.Network}
The total flow leaving $S$ --- sum over every arc with tail inside $S$
and head outside.  \textbf{!} This is \emph{not} the sum of the $f^{+}(v)$ over $v \in S$: arcs
internal to $S$ are counted there but not here.  Exercise 11.1.2 makes the exact
relationship precise, and it is the difference $f^{+} - f^{-}$ that behaves well.

\textbf{!} Missing from Mathlib.  A double \texttt{Finset.sum} over $S$ and
$S^{c}$, which the capacity-as-a-function carrier makes possible; $f u v = 0$ for a
non-arc contributes nothing.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[$f^{-}(S) = f(\bar{S}, S) = \sum_{u\notin S} \sum_{v\in S} f u v$]
\lean{Networks.Network.fIn}
\label{Networks.Network.fIn}
\leanok
\uses{Networks.Network}
The total flow entering $S$.  Conservation forces the resultant flow
out of every intermediate vertex to vanish, which is what makes the resultant flow
out of $X$ equal the resultant flow into $Y$ (exercise 11.1.3) and hence \texttt{val f}
well defined.

The mirror of \texttt{fOut} with the two sums swapped.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[A flow: (11.1) capacity constraint + (11.2) conservation at intermediate vertices]
\lean{Networks.Network.IsFlow}
\label{Networks.Network.IsFlow}
\leanok
\uses{Networks.Network, Networks.Network.I, Networks.Network.fIn, Networks.Network.fOut}
Nothing over-loaded, nothing accumulating.  The zero flow's existence
is what makes \texttt{exists\_maxFlow} non-vacuous.

The lower bound $0 \le f(a)$ of (11.1) is free: $f$ is $\mathbb{N}$-valued.
Conservation is stated as \texttt{fIn f \{v\} = fOut f \{v\}} on singletons, which unfolds to
the book's $f^{-}(v) = f^{+}(v)$ --- note \texttt{fIn}/\texttt{fOut} on a singleton are genuinely the
per-vertex quantities, since there are no arcs internal to a singleton.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[\texttt{val f = f$^{+}$(X) $-$ f$^{-}$(X)}]
\lean{Networks.Network.val}
\label{Networks.Network.val}
\leanok
\uses{Networks.Network, Networks.Network.fIn, Networks.Network.fOut}
The net rate at which the commodity travels from producers to
consumers.  Conservation at the intermediate vertices is what makes the two ways of
measuring it agree.

\textbf{!} \textbf{$\mathbb{Z}$-valued, and this is load-bearing.}  In $\mathbb{N}$ the
truncated subtraction would make exercise 11.1.2 --- the identity the whole chapter
rests on --- false, since individual terms $f^{+}(v) - f^{-}(v)$ are genuinely negative at
vertices absorbing more than they emit.  Every $f^{+} - f^{-}$ in this file is therefore
cast to $\mathbb{Z}$ before subtracting.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[A cut $(S, \bar{S})$ with $x \in S$, $y \notin S$]
\lean{Networks.Network.IsCut}
\label{Networks.Network.IsCut}
\leanok
\uses{Networks.Network}
A way of severing the network so the source is on one side and the
sink on the other.  Every unit of flow must cross every cut, which is why cuts
bound flows from above (theorem 11.1) --- and, more surprisingly, why the best cut
exactly matches the best flow (theorem 11.3).

\textbf{!} Missing from Mathlib.  Identified with the \emph{vertex set} $S$
rather than the arc set $(S, \bar{S})$, since $S$ determines the arcs and is far easier
to quantify over.  \texttt{capOf} then computes the arc set's capacity.  Note $y \notin S$ is
the book's $y \in \bar{S}$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[\texttt{cap (S, $\bar{S}$) = $\sum$\_\{u$\in$S\} $\sum$\_\{v$\notin$S\} c u v}]
\lean{Networks.Network.capOf}
\label{Networks.Network.capOf}
\leanok
\uses{Networks.Network}
The total throughput of the severed arcs --- how much traffic could at
most cross that divide.  Since all the flow must pass through, it bounds \texttt{val f}
above.

\textbf{!} Missing from Mathlib.  Structurally identical to \texttt{fOut} with
\texttt{cap} in place of $f$, which is exactly why theorem 11.1's proof is a two-line
comparison.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[A maximum flow]
\lean{Networks.Network.IsMaxFlow}
\label{Networks.Network.IsMaxFlow}
\leanok
\uses{Networks.Network, Networks.Network.IsFlow, Networks.Network.val}
Ship as much as the network allows.  Theorem 11.2 characterises these
as exactly the flows admitting no incrementing path --- the flow-theoretic analogue
of Berge's theorem 5.1 for matchings.

"No flow of larger value" is stated positively as
\texttt{$\forall$ f', IsFlow f' $\to$ val f' $\le$ val f}, which is the form every consumer wants.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[A minimum cut]
\lean{Networks.Network.IsMinCut}
\label{Networks.Network.IsMinCut}
\leanok
\uses{Networks.Network, Networks.Network.IsCut, Networks.Network.capOf}
The cheapest way to sever the network --- the bottleneck.  Theorem 11.3
says its capacity is exactly the maximum throughput.  B&M record the easy half
first: \emph{If $f}$ is a maximum flow and $\tilde{K}$ is a minimum cut, we have, as a special
case of theorem 11.1, that \texttt{val f\emph{ $\le$ cap $\tilde{K}$}} (11.8).

As with \texttt{IsMaxFlow}, stated positively.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[An $f$-incrementing path from the source]
\lean{Networks.Network.IncPath}
\label{Networks.Network.IncPath}
\leanok
\uses{Networks.Network}
A route from source to sink along which the flow can still be pushed
up.  Crucially it may travel \emph{against} an arc --- a \textbf{reverse arc} --- provided that
arc currently carries positive flow, which can then be cancelled.  This is what
lets the algorithm undo earlier bad choices, exactly as an augmenting path in
matching theory rearranges an existing matching; B&M make the analogy explicit:
*the r\^ole played by incrementing paths in flow theory is analogous to that of
augmenting paths in matching theory* (compare theorem 5.1).  The book's example is
figure 11.5(a), where $P = xv_{1}v_{2}v_{3}y$ is $f$-incrementing with $\iota(P) = 2$.

\textbf{!} Missing from Mathlib; an honest, complete inductive family ---
\emph{static}, not procedural.  \texttt{nil} starts at \texttt{N.x}; \texttt{fwd} extends along an
$f$-unsaturated arc (\texttt{f u v < cap u v}); \texttt{back} extends \emph{against} an $f$-positive
arc ($0 < f v u$).  The index is the current endpoint, so \texttt{N.IncPath f N.y} is
exactly an $f$-incrementing path.

\textbf{!} This is a directed \textbf{walk} --- repeated vertices are allowed --- not a path.  That
is deliberate and is what theorem 11.2's proof actually uses: the set $S$ of
vertices reachable by $f$-unsaturated \emph{walks} is what the cut is built from, and
restricting to paths would complicate the reachability closure for no gain.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[The residual capacity $\iota(P) > 0$ of an incrementing path --- a recursion over \texttt{IncPath}]
\lean{Networks.Network.IncPath.iota}
\label{Networks.Network.IncPath.iota}
\uses{Networks.Network, Networks.Network.IncPath}
The bottleneck along the path.  A forward arc has room $c(a) - f(a)$
left; a reverse arc can give back at most the $f(a)$ it currently carries.  The
smallest of these slacks is how much extra can be pushed through in one go.

\textbf{\textbf{!} Defective: this definition has a \texttt{sorry} body.}  $\iota(P)$ is therefore an opaque
natural number, not the bottleneck of anything.  Consequences: exercise 11.3.1
(\texttt{revisedFlow\_isFlow\_and\_val}) asserts \texttt{val $\hat{f}$ = val f + $\iota$(P)} about two opaque
constants and so says nothing, and the forward direction of theorem 11.2 --- which
needs $\iota(P) > 0$ to get a strictly better flow --- has no content to appeal to.
This also violates the project convention (\texttt{.claude/CLAUDE.md}): *never \texttt{sorry} in
a \texttt{def}*.

\emph{The repair} is a structural recursion over the \texttt{IncPath} family, carrying the
running minimum:

    iota nil          = $\top$ (or: recurse with an accumulator seeded at the first arc)
    iota (fwd P h)    = min (iota P) (cap u v - f u v)
    iota (back P h)   = min (iota P) (f v u)

The only wrinkle is \texttt{nil}, which has no arcs and so no minimum; either return a
sentinel and prove \texttt{0 < iota P} for non-\texttt{nil} paths, or index the recursion by a
running minimum passed in.  The second is cleaner and avoids $\mathbb{N}\infty$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[The revised flow $\hat{f}$ (11.9) obtained by pushing $\iota(P)$ along $P$]
\lean{Networks.Network.revisedFlow}
\label{Networks.Network.revisedFlow}
\uses{Networks.Network, Networks.Network.IncPath}
Push $\iota(P)$ more along every forward arc of the path and take $\iota(P)$
back off every reverse arc.  Conservation survives because at each interior vertex
the increase in and the increase out match; and the value rises by exactly $\iota(P)$
(exercise 11.3.1).  This is the engine of the labelling method: repeatedly find an
incrementing path and revise, until none exists --- at which point theorem 11.2
certifies maximality.

\textbf{\textbf{!} Defective: this definition has a \texttt{sorry} body.}  $\hat{f}$ is an opaque function, so
exercise 11.3.1 --- the only statement about it --- is vacuous, and theorem 11.2's
forward direction has nothing to revise with.  Same convention violation as
\texttt{iota}.

\emph{The repair} is a structural recursion over \texttt{IncPath} mirroring \texttt{iota}'s, adjusting
one arc per constructor:

    revisedFlow nil       = f
    revisedFlow (fwd P _) = Function.update$_{2}$ (revisedFlow P) u v (f u v + iota P)
    revisedFlow (back P _)= Function.update$_{2}$ (revisedFlow P) v u (f v u - iota P)

\textbf{!} Note \texttt{iota P} must be the bottleneck of the \textbf{whole} path, not of the prefix, or
the capacity constraint fails on early arcs --- so \texttt{iota} should be computed once and
threaded, rather than recomputed at each step.  That coupling is the reason both
definitions were deferred together, and it is why repairing \texttt{iota} first is the
right order.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Local minimal \texttt{edgeConnectivity $\kappa$'(G)} (repo has the real one)]
\lean{Networks.edgeConnectivity}
\label{Networks.edgeConnectivity}
\leanok
Corollary 11.5 relates it to edge-disjoint paths: $G$ is
$k$-edge-connected exactly when any two distinct vertices are joined by $k$
edge-disjoint paths --- the global connectivity number turned into a local path
count.

A minimal local copy; the real one lives in
\texttt{TCSlib.GraphTheory.Connectivity}, deliberately not imported so this file stands
alone.  \textbf{!} \texttt{sInf $\emptyset$ = 0}, so a graph with no edge cut (a one-vertex graph) gets
$\kappa' = 0$ --- a boundary case that will bite corollary 11.5 exactly as it bit
chapter 10's \texttt{associatedDigraph\_isKArcConnected\_iff}.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Local minimal \texttt{vertexConnectivity $\kappa$(G)} (repo has the real one)]
\lean{Networks.vertexConnectivity}
\label{Networks.vertexConnectivity}
\leanok
Corollary 11.7 relates it to internally-disjoint paths: $G$ with
$\nu \ge k + 1$ is $k$-connected exactly when any two distinct vertices are joined by
$k$ internally-disjoint paths.  This is the form of Menger's theorem \S{}3.2 announced
without proof.

A minimal local copy, as for \texttt{edgeConnectivity}.  The $\nu - 1$
branch is the book's convention for graphs with no vertex cut (complete graphs).
\textbf{!} Both \texttt{sInf} conventions bite at the boundaries --- see the outline.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Local minimal \texttt{InternallyDisjoint} (repo has the real one, \texttt{TwoConnected.lean:58})]
\lean{Networks.InternallyDisjoint}
\label{Networks.InternallyDisjoint}
\leanok
The paths share only their endpoints.  This is the notion in which
Menger's vertex theorem 11.7 and corollary 11.7 are phrased, and --- via the vertex
splitting of theorem 11.6 --- it is what \emph{arc}-disjointness in the split digraph
corresponds to.

A minimal local copy (the repo's is \texttt{TwoConnected.lean:58}),
stated for a \textbf{pair} of walks.  \textbf{!} Menger's theorem needs internal disjointness of a
whole \emph{family}; extending this pairwise predicate to families is part of what
\texttt{maxInternallyDisjointPaths} must do, and is one reason that count was stubbed.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Max number of arc-disjoint directed $(x,y)$-paths in a unit-ish \texttt{Network}]
\lean{Networks.Network.maxArcDisjointPaths}
\label{Networks.Network.maxArcDisjointPaths}
\uses{Networks.Network}
For a unit-capacity network this equals the value of a maximum flow:
each path carries one unit, and arc-disjointness is exactly the capacity
constraint.

\textbf{\textbf{!} \texttt{sorry} body.}  \emph{Repair:} \texttt{sSup} over $k$ such that there are $k$ directed
$(x,y)$-paths in the underlying digraph (arcs = pairs with \texttt{0 < cap u v}) that are
pairwise arc-disjoint.  Needs a directed-path notion; see the section note.
\end{definition}

For a unit-capacity network this equals the value of a maximum flow:

\textbf{\textbf{!} \texttt{sorry} body.}  \emph{Repair:} \texttt{sSup} over $k$ such that there are $k$ directed

\begin{definition}[Max number of arc-disjoint directed $(x,y)$-paths in a digraph]
\lean{Networks.maxArcDisjointDirectedPaths}
\label{Networks.maxArcDisjointDirectedPaths}
The left-hand side of Menger's arc theorem 11.4: how many routes from
$x$ to $y$ can run simultaneously without any two sharing an arc.

\textbf{\textbf{!} \texttt{sorry} body.}  \emph{Repair:} \texttt{sSup} over $k$ admitting $k$ pairwise arc-disjoint
directed $(x,y)$-paths.  Needs a directed-path notion (\texttt{Digraph.IsDirectedPath} in
the ch-10 file) \textbf{and} an arc-list, which is \texttt{arcsOf} there --- itself

The left-hand side of Menger's arc theorem 11.4: how many routes from

\begin{definition}[Min number of arcs destroying all directed $(x,y)$-paths in a digraph]
\lean{Networks.maxInternallyDisjointDirectedPaths}
\label{Networks.maxInternallyDisjointDirectedPaths}
The right-hand side of Menger's arc theorem 11.4: how few arcs must be
cut to sever $x$ from $y$ entirely.

\textbf{\textbf{!} \texttt{sorry} body.}  \emph{Repair:} \texttt{sInf \{k | $\exists$ Z : Finset (V $\times$ V), Z.card = k $\land$ $\lnot$ Relation.ReflTransGen (fun u v => D.Adj u v $\land$ (u,v) $\notin$ Z) x y\}}.

--- reachability suffices.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Max number of internally-disjoint directed $(x,y)$-paths in a digraph]
\lean{Networks.minVerticesDestroyingDirectedPaths}
\label{Networks.minVerticesDestroyingDirectedPaths}
The left-hand side of Menger's vertex theorem 11.6 --- routes sharing no
intermediate vertex, so destroying any one interior station leaves the others
intact.

\textbf{\textbf{!} \texttt{sorry} body.}  \emph{Repair:} as for the arc version but with internal-vertex
disjointness, which needs only the paths' vertex lists (\texttt{Quiver.Path.vertices}), not
\texttt{arcsOf} --- so it is easier than \texttt{maxArcDisjointDirectedPaths}.
\end{definition}

\lean{Networks.maxEdgeDisjointPaths}
\label{Networks.maxEdgeDisjointPaths}

\texttt{sSup \{k | $\exists$ ps : Fin k $\to$ G.Walk x y, ($\forall$ i, (ps i).IsPath) $\land$ $\forall$ i j, i $\ne$ j $\to$ List.Disjoint (ps i).edges (ps j).edges\}}.

\begin{definition}[Max number of vertex-disjoint $S$--$T$ paths (Ex 11.4.3)]
\lean{Networks.maxSTVertexDisjointPaths}
\label{Networks.maxSTVertexDisjointPaths}
The "fan" or set-to-set form of Menger's theorem, where the endpoints
are not fixed but merely constrained to lie in prescribed sets.  This is the form
exercise 11.4.4 (Dirac) actually consumes.

\textbf{\textbf{!} \texttt{sorry} body --- definable today.}  \emph{Repair:} \texttt{sSup} over $k$ admitting $k$
paths, each with one end in $S$ and one in $T$, pairwise \textbf{vertex}-disjoint (not
merely internally disjoint --- the endpoints must differ too, which is why this is not
a special case of \texttt{maxInternallyDisjointPaths}).  A $\Sigma$-typed family
\texttt{Fin k $\to$ $\Sigma$ u $\in$ S, $\Sigma$ v $\in$ T, G.Walk u v} handles the varying endpoints.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[The associated digraph $D(G)$: each edge becomes two opposite arcs (cited as ex 10.3.6)]
\lean{Networks.associatedDigraph}
\label{Networks.associatedDigraph}
Make every street two-way.  B&M call it \emph{a simple trick}: it is how
theorems 11.5 and 11.7 are deduced from their directed counterparts 11.4 and 11.6,
since paths in $G$ correspond exactly to directed paths in $D(G)$.

One line --- \texttt{G.Adj} is already symmetric, so it \emph{is} the arc
relation.  A local copy of chapter 10's \texttt{SimpleGraph.associatedDigraph}; the
path correspondence that makes the trick work is that file's
\texttt{associatedDigraph\_pathEquiv}, which is itself \texttt{sorry}-bodied there.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[The vertex-splitting digraph $D'$ of Theorem 11.6, on $V \oplus V$: \texttt{inl v = v'}, \texttt{inr v =\dots}]
\lean{Networks.splitDigraph}
\label{Networks.splitDigraph}
\leanok
Each vertex becomes a tiny one-way corridor $v' \to v''$, so *passing
through* $v$ now costs an arc.  This converts vertex-destruction into
arc-destruction, letting the vertex form of Menger's theorem be read off from the
arc form: *two directed $(x,y)$-paths in $D'$ are arc-disjoint if and only if the
corresponding paths in $D$ are internally-disjoint.*

\textbf{!} Missing from Mathlib.  Carrier $V \oplus V$, with \texttt{inl v = v'} and
\texttt{inr v = v''}; internal arcs are \texttt{inl u $\to$ inr v} when $u = v$, and original arcs
become \texttt{inr u $\to$ inl v}.

\textbf{!} \textbf{Simplified: it does not special-case $x$ and $y$.}  The book splits only
$V \ {x, y}$, leaving the endpoints intact; this splits \emph{every} vertex.  The
consequence is that $x$ and $y$ also acquire internal arcs, so a destroying set in
$D'$ could cut $x$'s or $y$'s own corridor --- which corresponds to deleting $x$ or
$y$ themselves, something the book's vertex-destruction forbids.  Statements about
\texttt{splitDigraph} therefore address \texttt{Sum.inr x} and \texttt{Sum.inl y} (the far ends of those
corridors), which sidesteps the issue for exercise 11.4.1; but the simplification
should be checked before it is relied on elsewhere.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[IsFeasible]
\lean{Networks.Network.IsFeasible}
\label{Networks.Network.IsFeasible}
\leanok
\uses{Networks.Network, Networks.Network.IsFlow, Networks.Network.fIn, Networks.Network.fOut}
for supplies $\sigma$ and demands \texttt{dem} (B&M's $\partial$). \textbf{!} MISSING. Honest def.

Nobody ships more than they can produce, and everybody receives at
least what they ordered.  Gale's theorem 11.8 characterises existence: for every
$S$, the capacity out of $S$ must cover the \emph{net} demand of $\bar{S}$.

\textbf{!} Missing from Mathlib.  \texttt{dem} is B&M's $\partial$.  Both conditions
are cast to $\mathbb{Z}$ before subtracting, for the reason recorded under \texttt{val}.  Supplies
and demands are $V \to \mathbb{N}$ total functions, with the conditions quantified only over
$X$ and $Y$, so their values elsewhere are irrelevant.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[$(p,q)$ is realisable by a simple bipartite graph: there is a $(0,1)$-matrix $B$ with row sums $p$ and\dots]
\lean{Networks.RealisableBipartite}
\label{Networks.RealisableBipartite}
\leanok
Can two prescribed lists of degrees occur as the two sides of a
bipartite graph?  The book's $p = (3,2,2,2,1)$, $q = (3,3,2,1,1)$ is realisable
(figure 11.12), whereas $p = q = (5,4,4,2,1)$ is not (exercise 11.5.2) even though
the sums agree.

\textbf{!} Missing from Mathlib (0 hits for Gale--Ryser).  Carried as a
$(0,1)$-\textbf{matrix} \texttt{B : Fin m $\to$ Fin n $\to$ Bool} rather than a bipartite \texttt{SimpleGraph},
following the book's own closing remark: *With each simple bipartite graph $G$ \dots
we can associate an $m \times n$ matrix $B$ in which $b_ij = 1$ or $0$, depending on
whether $x_{i}y_{j}$ is an edge of $G$ or not.  Conversely, every $m \times n$ $(0,1)$-matrix
corresponds in this way to a simple bipartite graph.*  The two are equivalent and
the matrix avoids constructing a graph on \texttt{Fin m $\oplus$ Fin n} with a bipartition proof.
Due to Ryser (1957).
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[$G$ is $(m,n)$-orientable: it admits an orientation in which every indegree is $m$ or $n$]
\lean{Networks.IsOrientable}
\label{Networks.IsOrientable}
\leanok
Make every edge one-way so each vertex ends up receiving exactly $m$
arrows, or exactly $n$.  Since $G$ is $(m+n)$-regular, indegree $m$ forces outdegree
$n$ and conversely, so an orientation splits the vertices into two classes.
Exercise 11.5.5(a) characterises orientability by a cut condition, and (b) shows the
classes can always be rebalanced one step towards each other.

\textbf{!} Missing from Mathlib (0 hits for "orientable").  The
orientation is spelled out inline as a \texttt{Digraph D} with three clauses --- $D \subseteq G$, $D$
never two-way, $D$ covers every edge --- rather than reusing chapter 10's
\texttt{IsOrientationOf}, which this file does not import.  The fourth clause is the
indegree condition.  Note the $(m+n)$-regularity is \emph{not} part of this definition;
it appears as a hypothesis on the theorems that use it.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[$|(S, \bar{S})|$: the number of edges of $G$ crossing the cut $(S, \bar{S})$ (Ex 11.5.5)]
\lean{Networks.edgeBoundaryCard}
\label{Networks.edgeBoundaryCard}
\leanok
The size of the undirected edge cut at $S$ --- how many edges would have
to be severed to separate $S$ from the rest.  In exercise 11.5.5(a) it is the
capacity available to carry the imbalance the prescribed indegrees force across
$S$'s boundary.

A double sum of indicators rather than a \texttt{Finset.card}, matching
the shape of \texttt{fOut}/\texttt{capOf} so the three compare directly.  Since \texttt{G.Adj} is
symmetric and the sum runs over $S \times S^{c}$, each crossing edge is counted \textbf{once}.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[sum_resultant_eq_fOut_sub_fIn]
\lean{Networks.sum_resultant_eq_fOut_sub_fIn}
\label{Networks.sum_resultant_eq_fOut_sub_fIn}
\leanok
\uses{Networks.Network, Networks.Network.fIn, Networks.Network.fOut}
Summing the \emph{net} outflow over the vertices of $S$ gives the net
outflow of $S$ as a whole.  The book flags the trap: *in general,
$\sum_{v \in S} f^{+}(v) \ne f^{+}(S)$ and $\sum_{v \in S} f^{-}(v) \ne f^{-}(S)$* --- only the difference
behaves, and only because the internal arcs cancel.

\textbf{*} \textbf{Build this first} --- lemma 11.1 and theorem 11.1 both rest on
it, and it is where the $\mathbb{Z}$-valuedness of \texttt{val} earns its keep: in $\mathbb{N}$ step 3's
cancellation is false, since $f^{+}{v} - f^{-}{v}$ truncates at each vertex individually.
Note it needs \textbf{no} \texttt{IsFlow} hypothesis: it is pure bookkeeping about an arbitrary
$f$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[fOut_X_sub_fIn_X_eq_fIn_Y_sub_fOut_Y]
\lean{Networks.fOut_X_sub_fIn_X_eq_fIn_Y_sub_fOut_Y}
\label{Networks.fOut_X_sub_fIn_X_eq_fIn_Y_sub_fOut_Y}
\leanok
\uses{Networks.Network, Networks.Network.IsFlow, Networks.Network.fIn, Networks.Network.fOut}
Whatever leaves the producers must arrive at the consumers.  This is
what makes \texttt{val f} well defined --- the two natural ways to measure throughput agree,
and the book \emph{defines} \texttt{val f} as the first only after asserting they coincide.

Step 4's $f^{+}(S) = f^{-}(S^{c})$ is worth an explicit \texttt{simp} lemma; it
recurs throughout the chapter.  Step 3 is where \texttt{N.hdisj} is spent.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[val_eq_fOut_sub_fIn]
\lean{Networks.val_eq_fOut_sub_fIn}
\label{Networks.val_eq_fOut_sub_fIn}
\leanok
\uses{Networks.Network, Networks.Network.IsCut, Networks.Network.IsFlow, Networks.Network.fIn, Networks.Network.fOut, Networks.Network.val}
The value of a flow can be measured across \emph{any} cut, not just at the
source: all the material has to cross somewhere, and nothing is lost in between.
This is the observation from which theorem 11.1 immediately follows.

\textbf{\textbf{!} Statement defect.}  This is \textbf{false as stated} --- the seam between \S{}11.1's
multi-source setting and \S{}11.2's single-source one.  B&M close it by fiat
(*throughout the next three sections, we shall confine our attention to networks
that have a single source $x$ and a single sink $y$*), but the \texttt{Network} structure
here relates $x$, $y$ to $X$, $Y$ in no way at all, so \texttt{val} (defined over $X$) and
the cut (separating $x$ from $y$) measure different things.  The three-vertex
counterexample is worked out in full in the \texttt{Network} docstring above.  \emph{The repair}
is the hypothesis \texttt{N.X = \{N.x\}} (with \texttt{N.Y = \{N.y\}}), either as a structure field or
on this statement.  \textbf{The skeleton assumes it} --- step 1 is not derivable without
it.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[val_le_capOf]
\lean{Networks.val_le_capOf}
\label{Networks.val_le_capOf}
\leanok
\uses{Networks.Network, Networks.Network.IsCut, Networks.Network.IsFlow, Networks.Network.capOf, Networks.Network.val}
Every unit shipped from $x$ to $y$ must squeeze through the cut, so no
flow can exceed the cut's throughput.  This weak-duality bound is half of the
max-flow min-cut theorem; the surprise of theorem 11.3 is that it is always
attained.  B&M record the special case immediately: \texttt{val f* $\le$ cap $\tilde{K}$} (11.8).
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[val_eq_capOf_iff]
\lean{Networks.val_eq_capOf_iff}
\label{Networks.val_eq_capOf_iff}
\leanok
\uses{Networks.Network, Networks.Network.IsCut, Networks.Network.IsFlow, Networks.Network.capOf, Networks.Network.val}
The cut is a genuine bottleneck precisely when it runs at full
capacity forwards and carries nothing backwards.  This characterisation is exactly
what the proof of theorem 11.2 verifies for the cut it constructs, which is why the
equality condition is worth stating separately rather than folding into theorem
11.1.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[isMaxFlow_and_isMinCut_of_val_eq_cap]
\lean{Networks.isMaxFlow_and_isMinCut_of_val_eq_cap}
\label{Networks.isMaxFlow_and_isMinCut_of_val_eq_cap}
\leanok
\uses{Networks.Network, Networks.Network.IsCut, Networks.Network.IsFlow, Networks.Network.IsMaxFlow, Networks.Network.IsMinCut, Networks.Network.capOf, Networks.Network.val}
The standard "weak duality certifies optimality" argument, the exact
analogue of lemma 5.3 for matchings and coverings.  It is what makes the labelling
method self-verifying: when the algorithm stops it produces a matching flow and cut,
and their equality proves both optimal.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[exists_maxFlow]
\lean{Networks.exists_maxFlow}
\label{Networks.exists_maxFlow}
\leanok
\uses{Networks.Network, Networks.Network.IsMaxFlow}
(assumed silently by the book).

Nothing deep: finitely many flows, so a best one.  Worth stating
separately because corollary 11.1 and theorem 11.3 both open by invoking it, and
because the zero flow is the only reason the set is nonempty.

Step 1 is where the $\mathbb{N}$-valued $f$ and finite $V$ pay off; note
theorem 11.1's bound is \emph{not} needed --- finiteness alone suffices, which is simpler
than the book's implicit reasoning and avoids the $X$/$x$ defect.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[exists_minCut]
\lean{Networks.exists_minCut}
\label{Networks.exists_minCut}
\leanok
\uses{Networks.Network, Networks.Network.IsMinCut}
(assumed silently by the book).

Finitely many subsets, at least one of them a cut, so a cheapest one.

\textbf{!} Step 1 needs \texttt{N.x $\ne$ N.y}, which the \texttt{Network} structure does
\textbf{not} provide --- \texttt{hdisj} separates $X$ from $Y$ but says nothing about $x$ and $y$.
This is a smaller instance of the structural gap recorded in the \texttt{Network}
docstring, and the same repair ($hx$, $hy$ tying $x$, $y$ to $X$, $Y$) supplies it,
since \texttt{hdisj} then forces $x \ne y$.  Without it the statement is false for a network
with $x = y$, where no cut exists.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[maxFlow_and_minCut_zero_of_no_path]
\lean{Networks.maxFlow_and_minCut_zero_of_no_path}
\label{Networks.maxFlow_and_minCut_zero_of_no_path}
\leanok
\uses{Networks.Network, Networks.Network.IsMaxFlow, Networks.Network.IsMinCut, Networks.Network.capOf, Networks.Network.val}
If the sink cannot be reached at all, nothing can be shipped and
nothing needs to be cut.

\textbf{!} Step 4 uses theorem 11.1, so it inherits the $X$/$x$ defect
recorded in the \texttt{Network} docstring; with the repair \texttt{N.X = \{N.x\}} it goes through.
The hypothesis is phrased with \texttt{ReflTransGen} over positive-capacity arcs rather
than as "no directed $(x,y)$-path", which is the same thing and needs no path
API.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[isMinCut_union_inter]
\lean{Networks.isMinCut_union_inter}
\label{Networks.isMinCut_union_inter}
\leanok
\uses{Networks.Network, Networks.Network.IsMinCut}
The minimum cuts form a lattice.  A consequence is that there is a
unique \emph{smallest} minimum cut and a unique \emph{largest} one, which is useful
algorithmically.

Unaffected by the $X$/$x$ defect --- the argument is entirely about
\texttt{capOf} and \texttt{IsCut}, never about \texttt{val}.  Step 2 is a good candidate to prove first
and independently.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[maxFlow_iff_no_incrementing_path]
\lean{Networks.maxFlow_iff_no_incrementing_path}
\label{Networks.maxFlow_iff_no_incrementing_path}
\uses{Networks.Network, Networks.Network.IncPath, Networks.Network.IsFlow, Networks.Network.IsMaxFlow}
B&M stress the analogy: *the r\^ole played by incrementing paths in flow
theory is analogous to that of augmenting paths in matching theory* --- compare
Berge's theorem 5.1.

Note steps 2--4 are exactly where \texttt{IncPath} being a \emph{walk} rather
than a path is convenient: $S$ is a reachability closure, and closure under \texttt{fwd}
and \texttt{back} is immediate for walks.  \textbf{!} Step 5 uses theorem 11.1 and corollary 11.1,
so it inherits the $X$/$x$ defect.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[exists_cut_of_no_incrementing_path]
\lean{Networks.exists_cut_of_no_incrementing_path}
\label{Networks.exists_cut_of_no_incrementing_path}
\leanok
\uses{Networks.Network, Networks.Network.IncPath, Networks.Network.IsCut, Networks.Network.IsFlow, Networks.Network.capOf, Networks.Network.val}
*If $N$ contains no
$f$-incrementing path, then there is a cut $K$ with \texttt{val f = cap K}.*

The constructive core of theorem 11.2's converse: the cut built from
the $f$-unsaturated reachability set has capacity exactly \texttt{val f}.

\textbf{*} This has to be \textbf{extracted separately} because theorem 11.2's
\emph{statement} asserts only maximality and discards the cut, while theorem 11.3 needs
the cut itself.  Fill this one first and derive theorem 11.2's converse from it,
rather than the other way round --- otherwise the reachability construction has to be
written twice.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[maxFlow_min_cut]
\lean{Networks.maxFlow_min_cut}
\label{Networks.maxFlow_min_cut}
\uses{Networks.Network, Networks.Network.IsMaxFlow, Networks.Network.IsMinCut, Networks.Network.capOf, Networks.Network.val}
Theorem 11.1 gave the easy half --- \texttt{val f $\le$ cap K} for every flow and
cut; this says the bound is always achieved, so the bottleneck is not merely an
upper limit but the exact answer.  B&M call it *of central importance in graph
theory\emph{: }many results on graphs turn out to be easy consequences of this theorem as
applied to suitably chosen networks*, as \S{}\S{}11.4 and 11.5 demonstrate with Menger's
theorems and the Gale--Ryser criterion.

\emph{The labelling method} (Ford and Fulkerson, 1957), which the constructive proof
yields: start from the zero flow and repeatedly grow an $f$-unsaturated tree from
$x$, until either it reaches $y$ (\textbf{breakthrough}, giving an incrementing path to
revise along) or it stops growing (certifying maximality by theorem 11.2).  B&M note
it is \emph{not} a good algorithm --- figure 11.9 gives a network needing $2m + 1$
iterations for arbitrary $m$ --- but Edmonds and Karp (1970) showed that scanning
"first-labelled first-scanned", i.e. always taking a \emph{shortest} incrementing path,
makes it good.

Steps 1--4 are all already-stated results, so this theorem is
five lines once its inputs are filled --- but it sits at the top of the dependency
chain and inherits every defect below it, including the \texttt{sorry}-bodied $\iota$ and
\texttt{revisedFlow} via step 2.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[unitCapacity_maxFlow_eq_arcDisjoint]
\lean{Networks.unitCapacity_maxFlow_eq_arcDisjoint}
\label{Networks.unitCapacity_maxFlow_eq_arcDisjoint}
\uses{Networks.Network, Networks.Network.IsMaxFlow, Networks.Network.maxArcDisjointPaths, Networks.Network.val}
With unit capacities a flow \emph{is} a packing of arc-disjoint routes, each
carrying one unit.  This lemma is the bridge from flow theory to Menger.

\textbf{!} Two imported dependencies, both currently defective: step 1
needs chapter 10's exercise 10.3.3, whose statement there mentions the
\texttt{sorry}-bodied \texttt{arcsOf}; and B&M's proof of \emph{that} exercise adds $l$ parallel arcs,
which neither \texttt{Digraph} nor this file's \texttt{cap : V $\to$ V $\to$ $\mathbb{N}$} carrier can express.  \textbf{!}
Also note \texttt{hunit : $\forall$ u v, cap u v $\le$ 1} permits \texttt{cap = 0}, i.e. absent arcs, which is
what the book means by "each arc has unit capacity"; that reading is correct here.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[unitCapacity_minCut_eq_minDestroying]
\lean{Networks.unitCapacity_minCut_eq_minDestroying}
\label{Networks.unitCapacity_minCut_eq_minDestroying}
\uses{Networks.Network, Networks.Network.IsMinCut, Networks.Network.capOf, Networks.Network.minArcsDestroyingPaths}
With part (a) and the max-flow min-cut theorem, this immediately yields
Menger's arc theorem 11.4 --- the whole of \S{}11.4 rests on these two halves.

\textbf{!} Step 1 uses that with unit capacities \texttt{cap S} counts arcs; this
needs \texttt{hunit} \emph{and} that every counted arc actually exists (\texttt{cap u v = 1}, not $0$),
so the sum-to-cardinality step deserves care.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[menger_arc_digraph]
\lean{Networks.menger_arc_digraph}
\label{Networks.menger_arc_digraph}
\uses{Networks.maxArcDisjointDirectedPaths, Networks.minArcsDestroyingDirectedPaths}
The number of independent routes you can run equals the number of links
an adversary must cut to stop you.  This is the first of the four Menger theorems
the chapter derives --- arc/edge and vertex versions, for digraphs and graphs --- two of
which were quoted without proof back in \S{}3.2.

\textbf{!} Steps 2 and 3 are not free: the network-level counts
(\texttt{Network.maxArcDisjointPaths}) and the digraph-level ones
(\texttt{maxArcDisjointDirectedPaths}) are \emph{separate} stubbed definitions, so once both are
repaired a lemma identifying them across the construction of step 1 will be needed.
Defining the network-level pair \emph{in terms of} the digraph-level pair applied to the
underlying digraph would make steps 2--3 definitional and is the better design.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[menger_edge_graph]
\lean{Networks.menger_edge_graph}
\label{Networks.menger_edge_graph}
\uses{Networks.maxEdgeDisjointPaths, Networks.minEdgesDestroyingPaths}
The undirected Menger theorem quoted in \S{}3.2 as the edge analogue of
Whitney's theorem 3.2.

Step 2's caveat is the one place where "a simple trick
immediately yields" is doing real work; budget for it.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[k_edge_connected_iff_edge_disjoint_paths]
\lean{Networks.k_edge_connected_iff_edge_disjoint_paths}
\label{Networks.k_edge_connected_iff_edge_disjoint_paths}
\uses{Networks.edgeConnectivity, Networks.maxEdgeDisjointPaths}
$k$-edge-connectedness says no $k - 1$ edges disconnect the graph; by
theorem 11.5 the minimum number of edges separating a \emph{specific} pair equals the
maximum number of edge-disjoint paths between them.  Minimising over pairs converts
the global statement into the local one.  This is the edge form of Menger's theorem
quoted without proof in \S{}3.2, generalising exercise 3.2.1 ($k = 2$) to all $k$.

Uses the local \texttt{edgeConnectivity} copy.  \textbf{!} Watch the \texttt{sInf $\emptyset$ = 0}
boundary flagged there: on a one-vertex graph no edge cut exists, so
\texttt{edgeConnectivity = 0}, while the right-hand side is vacuously true for every $k$
(there is no pair $u \ne v$).  So the $\leftrightarrow$ fails at $k \ge 1$, \texttt{card V $\le$ 1} --- a
\texttt{[Nontrivial V]} hypothesis is the fix, exactly as in chapter 10's
\texttt{associatedDigraph\_isKArcConnected\_iff}.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[menger_vertex_digraph]
\lean{Networks.menger_vertex_digraph}
\label{Networks.menger_vertex_digraph}
\uses{Networks.maxInternallyDisjointDirectedPaths, Networks.minVerticesDestroyingDirectedPaths}
\textbf{!} The hypothesis \texttt{$\lnot$ D.Adj x y} is load-bearing: an arc $(x, y)$ cannot
be destroyed by deleting \emph{intermediate} vertices, so without it the right-hand side
would be unattainable while the left is at least $1$.

\textbf{!} Step 1 must contend with \texttt{splitDigraph} splitting $x$ and $y$
as well, contrary to the book --- see that definition's docstring.  Concretely, a
$D'$-path from \texttt{inr x} to \texttt{inl y} never traverses $x$'s or $y$'s corridor, so the
correspondence is unharmed; but that fact needs stating rather than assuming.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[menger_vertex_graph]
\lean{Networks.menger_vertex_graph}
\label{Networks.menger_vertex_graph}
\uses{Networks.maxInternallyDisjointPaths, Networks.minVerticesDestroyingPaths}
The most quoted form of Menger's theorem, and the one \S{}3.2 announced
without proof.  The number of independent routes between two stations equals the
number of intermediate stations an adversary must destroy to sever them --- the vertex
analogue of max-flow min-cut duality, specialising at $k = 2$ to Whitney's theorem
3.2.

Note step 2 is genuinely easier than the corresponding step of
theorem 11.5, so this is the better of the two undirected Menger theorems to attempt
first.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[k_connected_iff_internally_disjoint_paths]
\lean{Networks.k_connected_iff_internally_disjoint_paths}
\label{Networks.k_connected_iff_internally_disjoint_paths}
\uses{Networks.maxInternallyDisjointPaths, Networks.vertexConnectivity}
$k$-connectivity says no $k - 1$ vertices disconnect the graph; theorem
11.7 converts the local separation number for a nonadjacent pair into a path count,
and minimising over pairs converts global into local.

\textbf{!} B&M call this \emph{immediate}; it is not --- step 2 is genuine work,
and the $k = 2$ case alone is a full proof in the repo (\texttt{TwoConnected.lean:537}).
Uses the local \texttt{vertexConnectivity}, whose $\nu - 1$ fallback for complete graphs
interacts with step 2 (a complete graph has \emph{only} adjacent pairs), so check that
boundary.  \texttt{h : k + 1 $\le$ card V} is the book's $\nu \ge k + 1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[dirac_k_vertices_on_cycle]
\lean{Networks.dirac_k_vertices_on_cycle}
\label{Networks.dirac_k_vertices_on_cycle}
\uses{Networks.vertexConnectivity}
High connectivity forces any prescribed set of $k$ vertices onto a
single cycle.  For $k = 2$ this is corollary 3.2.1 --- in a 2-connected graph any two
vertices lie on a common cycle.  One of the classic applications of Menger's
theorem, illustrating B&M's remark that *many results on graphs turn out to be easy
consequences* of max-flow min-cut.

Depends on exercise 11.4.3, hence on two \texttt{sorry}-bodied
definitions; but note the \emph{statement} here mentions none of them --- it is about
\texttt{Walk}/\texttt{IsCycle} only, so it is well-formed and would be meaningful once its
dependency is repaired.  Among the \S{}11.4 items, this is the one whose statement is
already honest.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[gale_feasible_flow]
\lean{Networks.gale_feasible_flow}
\label{Networks.gale_feasible_flow}
\leanok
\uses{Networks.Network, Networks.Network.IsFeasible, Networks.Network.capOf}
A feasible flow exists exactly when, for every way of splitting the
vertices, the capacity available for shipping into $\bar{S}$ covers the \emph{net} demand there
--- the demand of the sinks in $\bar{S}$ less whatever supply already sits inside $\bar{S}$.
Necessity is obvious (that much material must cross the boundary); the content is
sufficiency.

\textbf{!} Steps 3--4 use corollary 11.1 and theorem 11.3, both currently
false for want of the \texttt{N.X = \{N.x\}} link --- though note $N'$ is built with a genuine
single source and sink, so the repair is satisfied \emph{there}; the defect bites only if
one tries to apply those results to $N$ itself.  Step 1's construction is the
largest single piece of work in \S{}11.5.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[galeRyser_realisable]
\lean{Networks.galeRyser_realisable}
\label{Networks.galeRyser_realisable}
\leanok
\uses{Networks.RealisableBipartite}
Equal sums (11.16) are necessary --- both count the edges --- but not
sufficient, as $p = q = (5,4,4,2,1)$ shows.  Condition (11.18) adds that the $k$
largest demands can actually be met: each $x_{i}$ can supply at most \texttt{min\{p$_{i}$, k\}} of
them, having only $p_{i}$ edges and only $k$ targets.

\emph{Matrix form.}  Let $B*$ have its first $p_{i}$ entries of row $i$ equal to $1$, and let
$p*$ be its column sums --- the \textbf{conjugate} of $p$ (that of $(5,4,4,2,1)$ is
$(5,4,3,3,1)$).  Row $i$ contributes \texttt{min\{p$_{i}$, k\}} to $\sum_{j\le k} p*_{j}$, so (11.18) says
exactly $\sum_{j\le k} p*_{j} \ge \sum_{j\le k} q_{j}$ --- the conjugate of $p$ dominates $q$.  Due to
Ryser (1957).

The chapter's hardest item.  $k$ is a \texttt{Fin n} and the book's
$1 \le k \le n$ becomes \texttt{k.val + 1} in the \texttt{min}, so check the off-by-one against the
book when filling.  The $(0,1)$-matrix carrier is used rather than a bipartite-graph
predicate; see \texttt{RealisableBipartite}.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[realisable_iff_reduced]
\lean{Networks.realisable_iff_reduced}
\label{Networks.realisable_iff_reduced}
\leanok
\uses{Networks.RealisableBipartite}
The bipartite analogue of the Havel--Hakimi reduction for degree
sequences (exercise 1.5.7): the vertex $x_{1}$ may as well spend its $p_{1}$ edges on the
$p_{1}$ highest-demand vertices of $Y$.  Part (b) --- dropped here as procedural --- turns
this into a construction algorithm.

\textbf{!} Two departures, both flagged in the source comment.  (i) $q'$
uses \textbf{truncated} natural subtraction ($q j - 1$ is $0$ when $q j = 0$), which is
harmless only because a realisable $q$ has $q j \ge 1$ wherever row $0$ puts an edge ---
worth checking rather than assuming.  (ii) B&M's $q'$ is \textbf{re-sorted} into
nonincreasing order, which this statement elides; without re-sorting, $q'$ need not
satisfy (11.17), so this reduction cannot be chained with theorem 11.9 as the book
intends.  If the intent is to iterate the reduction, the re-sorting must be
restored.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[isOrientable_iff_exists_partition]
\lean{Networks.isOrientable_iff_exists_partition}
\label{Networks.isOrientable_iff_exists_partition}
\leanok
\uses{Networks.IsOrientable, Networks.edgeBoundaryCard}
An $(m+n)$-regular graph is to be oriented so every indegree is $m$ or
$n$.  The partition names in advance which vertices get which, and the inequality is
a feasibility condition in Gale's sense.

\textbf{!} Step 2 needs an \textbf{eulerian orientation}, which comes from
chapters 4 and 10 (every graph with all degrees even has an Euler tour; orient along
it) --- a genuine import, absent from this file.  Note $(m+n)$-regular forces every
degree even only when $m + n$ is even, so the eulerian step may itself need the
odd-degree patch of chapter 10's exercise 10.1.10.  The absolute value is written as
a \textbf{two-sided bound} to avoid \texttt{abs} and keep the arithmetic in $\mathbb{Z}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[isOrientable_pred_succ]
\lean{Networks.isOrientable_pred_succ}
\label{Networks.isOrientable_pred_succ}
\leanok
\uses{Networks.IsOrientable}
The two permitted indegrees can always be moved one step closer
together.  Iterating, an $(m,n)$-orientable graph is $(m',n')$-orientable for every
admissible pair with $m' + n' = m + n$ and $|m' - n'| \le |m - n|$ --- in particular the
most balanced orientation is always available.

A short deduction \emph{given} part (a), which is the starred and
substantial half.  Step 2's "scales down" should be checked at the sign: the bound
is two-sided, so both directions shrink only because $|m - n - 2| \le |m - n|$ when
$m - n \ge 1$.
\end{theorem}
